title: I think you should almost never use AI to write
dot:
digraph G{graph[rankdir=TB, bgcolor="#f8f9fa", pad=0.5, nodesep=0.6, ranksep=0.8, fontname="Helvetica"];node[shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=11, margin=0.25];edge[color="#4a6fa5", penwidth=1.4, arrowsize=0.9, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10, fontcolor="#4a6fa5"];claim[label=< Almost never use AI to write
Substantive text: blog, report, memo,
thoughtful email, novel, analysis.
Even with detailed bullets and edits.
Current / near-future AI. >, fillcolor="#ffe8c2", color="#d4751e", penwidth=1.7];reasons[shape=plaintext, label=<
1. Writing is thinking
Drafting exposes holes in your argument
and forces you to change your mind.
Outsourcing the text lets you skip the thinking.
2. AI text is vague & subtly wrong
Confident prose hides empty or misleading
claims — hard to spot without real expertise.
Example: AI chip smuggling paragraph was
plausible but full of questionable choices.
3. Unlabeled AI writing is rude & misleading
Readers expect your thoughts and effort.
Undisclosed AI breaks the reader-writer
contract and lowers trust.
>];caveat[shape=plaintext, label=<
Not anti-AI — know the line
Use AI for transcription, data analysis,
search, brainstorming, feedback, and editing
(with human approval).
If you include AI text, label it
Readers can discount or vet it as needed.
Still avoid
Full substantive AI drafts, even labeled —
worse result and fewer readers.
>];bottom[label=< Bottom line
Write yourself to think clearly.
Use AI around the edges,
not for the core thinking/writing. >, fillcolor="#d9ead3", color="#3d7a3a", penwidth=1.7];claim->reasons[label="why?"];reasons->caveat[label="but"];caveat->bottom[label="so"];}
